column3: It closely parallels the focus's believing community, adding enduring God-consciousness as its lived quality.
The immediately preceding promise of no fear or grief frames the security given to the people identified in the focus.
It directly distinguishes professed submission from faith that has truly entered the heart, clarifying the focus's paired terms.
It depicts believers saved for their piety, supporting the focus's faithful community without its submission or sign language.
The local contrast with the God-conscious directly prepares the protected community named in the following verses.
Its warning to believers about betrayal concerns faithful conduct, but not belief in signs joined to submission.
It portrays the rescue of believing, God-conscious people, a partial parallel to the focus's community.
The immediately preceding address promises security, and the focus specifies its recipients as believers who were Muslims.
It explicitly relates Islam to God's guidance into faith and rejects treating that transition as human self-credit.
The future wish of disbelievers to have been Muslims provides a consequential contrast to the focus's fulfilled identity.
Its local judgment of wrongdoers sharing punishment contrasts with the faithful Muslims who follow in the passage.
The disciples explicitly answer the call to believe by testifying that they are Muslims.
Its summons to come in submission illustrates Muslim identity as yielding a proud claim to rule.
Patience amid hostility offers only a broad pastoral context for the focus's believing community.
The compelled surrender of false claimants contrasts with the voluntary submission attributed to the focus's believers.
It joins commitment to God's signs with settled certainty, directly reinforcing a principal feature of the focus.
The description of worldly furnishings does not clarify belief in signs or submission.
The repeated greeting of peace is not evidence for the focus's belief-and-submission identity.
It assigns the better final reward to believers who are God-conscious, a partial outcome parallel.
Its freedom from fear and grief supports the blessed outcome surrounding the focus, without defining its qualifying response.
The command to be among the first Muslims supports submission to God, though it does not mention belief in His signs.
Those threatened for believing in their Lord's signs ask to die as Muslims, explicitly combining both elements of the focus.
The later local instruction to part with peace sets a contrasting response to persistent refusal in the same surah.
The call to submit follows the proclamation of one God, directly presenting the response named in the focus.
It gives the inverse of the focus: denial of God's signs and lack of faith leading to destruction.
It promises that God does not waste the reward of believers, supporting the favorable horizon of the focus.
Its challenge asks what message people will believe after this one, sharpening the focus's positive belief in signs.
It contrasts believers in God and His messengers with those who deny God's signs and face the Fire.
The local rejection of rival worship supplies the monotheistic ground for the submission named in the focus.
Under threat, the believers' faith increases together with submission, directly linking the two dispositions.
The hearers profess faith in the recitation while identifying themselves as already Muslims.
Clinging to an inherited book explains a rival posture in the local polemic but not the focus's qualifying response.
Entering in peace describes a final state rather than belief in signs or submission.
It presents the opposite response: arrogance produces refusal of God's signs and failure to believe them.
The good news in this life and the next extends the assurance associated with the believing community.
The rebuke for scant belief provides a direct negative contrast to the focus's settled belief.
Pride before God's signs illustrates the refusal opposed to the focus's believing reception of them.
The local command to hold fast to revelation gives the practical fidelity that supports belief in God's signs.
The merciful greeting of peace echoes the focus's favorable setting only at a distance.
Its arrogant denial of God's signs supplies a clear contrast to the focus's believers in those signs.
It connects belief and righteous practice with secure monotheistic worship, a broad lived-submission parallel.
Their compelled surrender on the Day of Judgment contrasts with the focus's voluntary Muslim identity.
Moses explicitly joins belief in God with being Muslims and makes reliance on God their practical expression.
The local proclamation of one Lord, worship, and the straight path grounds the submission attributed to the focus's people.
Security from fear is a remote lexical association, not the focus's belief in signs or submission.
It identifies those who disbelieve in God's signs as the companions of the left, the focus's direct opposite.
The rescue of believers supports the favorable distinction of the focus without its signs-and-submission pairing.
The wrongdoers' forced surrender and false denial contrasts with sincere submission joined to belief.
Its emphatic denial of God's signs forms the direct negative counterpart to the focus's belief in them.
This local reaction to a false comparison does not materially clarify the focus's believing Muslims.
The command to submit to the one God presents the central response named in the focus.
It states that the faithful are those who believe in their Lord's signs, directly matching the focus's first qualification.
Abraham's affiliation with an earlier community does not clarify belief in signs or submission.
The queen's admission of self-wrong and submission to God illustrates a concrete transition into Islam.
The historical punishment and route description do not develop the focus's response to God's signs.
The immediately following description of lasting Paradise supplies the reward setting for the people named in the focus.
It explicitly describes those who believe in God's signs as Muslims, nearly repeating the focus's formulation.
Belief in revealed scripture and certainty in the Hereafter support the focus's faithful reception of divine signs.
It addresses believers' distress and trust, but does not develop belief in signs or submission.
The queen's prior knowledge and Muslim identity offer a narrative instance of prepared submission.
Wronging God's signs brings self-loss, the direct inverse of the focus's believing response.
The local argumentative comparison does not itself establish belief in signs or submission.
A distress-driven claim of belief is only a limited contrast to the focus's established identity.
It contrasts the saved community with those who denied God's signs and were not believers.
A sound heart may accompany faithful submission, but the verse does not state the focus's belief in signs.
The command to be first among Muslims supports the focus's submission dimension.
It explicitly makes belief in God's signs the condition of being Muslims.
The local declaration of God as deity in heaven and earth provides the monotheistic basis for submission.
Its witness to persecution of believers concerns their social condition, not their belief in signs and submission.
It presents the opposite trajectory: evil ends in denial and mockery of God's signs.
Pharaoh's boast of dominion does not clarify the focus's faithful Muslim identity.
The immediate response to God's command, 'Submit,' gives a concise model of the focus's submission.
The verse concerns sectarian division rather than belief in God's signs or Muslim submission.
The account of Pharaoh's people obeying him does not illuminate the focus's qualifying response.
The anticipated arrival as Muslims situates submission within the queen's turning from sovereign self-rule.
It commands belief in confirming revelation and warns against disbelief in God's signs.
Turning from the Merciful's remembrance and acquiring a companion does not directly clarify the focus's formulation.
The greeting to the companions of the right is a distant outcome parallel, not evidence for the focus's response.
It distinguishes genuine believers from hypocrites, supporting the focus's stable identity claim.
The question about withholding the reminder from an excessive people does not define belief in signs or submission.
It sharply contrasts Muslims with criminals, reinforcing the moral distinction assumed by the focus.
The covered eyes and inability to hear do not specifically develop belief in God's signs or submission.
The local question about guiding the deaf and blind does not itself identify the focus's faithful response.
Calling to God, righteous action, and declaring oneself Muslim portray lived submission without the signs language.
It gives the punitive opposite of the focus: those who disbelieve in God's signs enter the Fire.
It contrasts Muslims with the unjust and links submission to seeking right guidance.
It identifies denial of God's signs and disbelief in the Hereafter as a contrary path to the focus.
It joins turning oneself to God with good action and the promise of no fear or grief.
Its condemnation of religious fragmentation does not materially define the focus's belief-and-submission pairing.
It makes remaining Muslim until death an enduring communal charge, extending the focus's identity through life.
Its warning against associating partners with God is only an indirect contrast to faithful submission.
Rightly receiving the Book culminates in believing it, clarifying faithful response to divine revelation.
Earlier peoples' denial of messengers supplies a historical contrast to the focus's believing community.
It names Abraham among God's believing servants, a partial personal parallel to the focus.
The rhetorical recollection of punishment does not clarify belief in signs or submission.
It names believers as bearers of honor, but does not develop their response to God's signs.
The gift of the Book as guidance supplies a broad revelation context without the focus's response language.
Its defining failure to believe in God is the direct inverse of the focus's faithful identity.
It assigns recompense to disbelief, supplying a general consequential contrast to the focus.
It identifies persistent refusal to believe as the condition opposed to the focus's settled belief.
Abraham and Ishmael ask that they and their descendants become a community submitted to God, a foundational communal parallel to the focus.
It combines belief in God's revelations and messengers with the declaration, 'we are Muslims.'
The believers' comprehensive faith in God, angels, books, and messengers supplies a broad revelation-belief parallel.
Jesus' helpers profess faith in God and ask to be witnessed as Muslims.
The shared call to worship one God concludes with a public declaration of Muslim submission.
It commands comprehensive belief in revelation and ends by declaring, 'we are Muslims.'
It makes remaining Muslim until death the enduring form of faithful communal commitment.
It commands believers to sustain faith in God, His messenger, and the revealed books, directly extending the focus's belief dimension.
It promises reward to those who believe in God and all His messengers without distinction.
It describes prophets who submitted to God while judging by the revealed Torah, linking submission with fidelity to revelation.
It explicitly addresses those who believe in God's signs, directly matching the focus's first qualification.
It rejects turning away from God and states the command to submit to the Lord of all worlds.
The declaration of exclusive worship culminates in being commanded as the first of the Muslims.
It defines believers by increased faith when God's signs are recited to them, a direct response-to-signs parallel.
Noah identifies his reward with God and states that he has been commanded to be among the Muslims.
After the challenge concerning revelation, it asks whether the hearers will submit.
Joseph joins gratitude for God's signs and authority with the prayer to die as a Muslim.
The Holy Spirit brings down the truth to strengthen believers and as guidance and good news for Muslims.
It states that Pharaoh was shown all God's signs but denied and refused them, the focus's direct opposite.
It names the community Muslims and calls them to strive faithfully for God.
It declares belief in what was revealed to both communities and concludes that their God is one and 'we are Muslims.'
It explicitly identifies those who believe in God's signs by their receptive, worshipful response when reminded of them.
It pairs Muslim men and women with believing men and women, showing the two identities as mutually reinforcing.
It commands turning back to God and submitting before punishment, presenting the active response named in the focus.
After the clear signs come, it rejects rival worship and states the command to submit to the Lord of the worlds.
It condemns one who hears God's signs and persists arrogantly in disbelief, the direct inverse of the focus's response.
The prayer of repentance and righteous intent ends with the declaration of being among the Muslims.
It commands belief in God, His messenger, and the light He sent down, a close revelation-and-faith parallel.
It pairs Muslim women with believing women in its description of devoted servants.
